tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Success depends of careful practice before the recital.
She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.
They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.
Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.
He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Success depends of careful practice before the recital.**

Depend never partners with of in standard English. The locked pattern is depend on (or upon) plus a noun or gerund for the thing that controls the outcome.
**B) She is responsible of watering the neighbour's plants.**

Responsible takes for when you name a duty or job. Responsible of is not an English ownership/duty frame.
**C) They are interested on learning Portuguese this summer.**

Interest as an adjective locks to in: interested in learning / interested in Portuguese.
**D) Despite of the rain, the picnic went ahead.**

Despite is a single preposition; it never takes of. You can write Despite the rain or In spite of the rain — but not Despite of.
**E) He was accused of cheating in the board-game tournament.**

Accuse (and be accused) locks to of plus a wrongdoing noun or gerund. Here accused of cheating is exactly the exam pattern.

Nothing to repair — keep of and the -ing form together.
tasks.solution_overview:
Before a recital or a neighbour-sitting favour, English often locks a verb or adjective to one preposition — and the wrong partner sounds almost right if you translate from another language.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This task is all about fixed dependency and responsibility patterns: depend on, responsible for, interested in, despite (no of), and accused of. The classic false friends are of after depend/responsible/despite, and on after interested.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline the head word and the preposition right after it. Ask whether that pair is the textbook lock for this meaning. If you can swap in the standard preposition and the sentence suddenly sounds native, mark the original false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.
Her recipe differs of last year's version.
We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.
The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.
She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He insisted on seeing the raw score sheets.**

Insist on plus a gerund is the fixed forcefulness pattern: he insisted on seeing the sheets, not a bare infinitive.

The form matches the lock, so the line stands.
**B) Her recipe differs of last year's version.**

Differ compares one thing with another using from. Differs of is a transfer error, not a variant.
**C) We apologised about spilling juice on the carpet.**

Careful exam English wants apologise for a fault or inconvenience. Apologised about is weaker and often marked wrong even when it is heard in speech.
**D) The documentary focuses to ocean plastics.**

Focus and concentrate take on, never to, when they name a topic of attention.
**E) She participated in the weekend pottery workshop.**

Participate in correctly names involvement in an event or activity. The workshop line uses the right lock.
tasks.solution_overview:
These lines mix everyday insist, differ, apologise, focus, and participate — verbs that almost all students know, but that each demand one locked preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch insist on + -ing, differ from, apologise for, focus on, and participate in. The traps swap of/about/to into slots that English does not allow for those heads.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the verb, then name the preposition that textbooks glue to it. If the sentence uses a different satellite, it is false even when the meaning is clear.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.
The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.
She is good in swimming long distances.
We look forward to meeting your cousins.
He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.
tactical_explanations:
**A) They objected against the new quiet-hours rule.**

Object takes to, not against: objected to the new quiet-hours rule. Protest against is a different verb with a different preposition.
**B) The volunteer is capable of handling the front desk.**

Capable of plus a gerund is the standard ability frame, and handling the front desk fits it cleanly.

Do not confuse it with able to + infinitive — different head, different pattern.
**C) She is good in swimming long distances.**

Skills and activities take good at in exam English: good at swimming. Good in is reserved (at best) for school subjects in some varieties, and even there at is safer for a sport/skill.
**D) We look forward to meeting your cousins.**

Look forward to is a multi-word unit; to is a preposition here, so it takes a noun or gerund (meeting), not a bare infinitive.

The cousins line is correctly formed.
**E) He succeeded to repair the bicycle chain.**

Succeed in plus -ing reports achievement. Succeeded to repair copies manage to, which is the wrong head for this verb.
tasks.solution_overview:
Object, capable, good, look forward, and succeed all look friendly — until the wrong preposition or infinitive slips in after them.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

The fixed frames here are object to, capable of + -ing, good at (skills), look forward to + -ing, and succeed in + -ing. Mixing against/in/to-infinitives against those locks is the trap set.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check two layers: which preposition the head wants, and whether what follows should be a gerund rather than a bare or to-infinitive.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.
This jacket belongs to my older brother.
You can rely of her to bring the tent.
They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.
A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The salad consists from tomatoes, cucumber, and feta.**

Consist of lists the ingredients or parts. Consist from has no place in this frame (be made from is a different pattern).
**B) This jacket belongs to my older brother.**

Belong to marks ownership cleanly: the jacket belongs to my older brother.

Never write belong of.
**C) You can rely of her to bring the tent.**

Rely, depend, and count all take on for trust. Rely of is the same transfer trap as depend of.
**D) They complained for the noisy neighbours upstairs.**

You complain about a problem (noise, service) and complain to a person. Complain for is non-standard for this meaning.
**E) A locked gate prevented them from entering the park.**

Prevent someone from + gerund is the restraint lock. The locked-gate line uses it correctly.

Do not replace from with to after prevent.
tasks.solution_overview:
Ownership, composition, trust, complaint, and prevention verbs are tightly glued to one preposition each in everyday English.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Target consist of, belong to, rely on, complain about, and prevent from. Swapping from/of/for into those slots is enough to fail the item.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the preposition names parts, possession, support, a grievance topic, or a blocked action — then match the lock listed above.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.
This trail is similar with the one near the lake.
My playlist is different than yours in every genre.
She has been married with her partner for twelve years.
The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Lisbon is famous for its tiled façades.**

Famous for plus a feature is the standard reputation pattern, and tiled façades fit that slot.

Famous as would name a role, not a tourist trademark.
**B) This trail is similar with the one near the lake.**

Similar, identical, and comparable take to, not with.
**C) My playlist is different than yours in every genre.**

In careful exam English prefer different from (or different to in some BrE); different than is often marked down even where American speech allows it.
**D) She has been married with her partner for twelve years.**

Married to a person is the lock. Married with copies other languages and belongs instead in frames like live with.
**E) The children are afraid of thunderstorms at night.**

Afraid of plus a noun (thunderstorms) is correct and natural.

Frightened of follows the same of pattern.
tasks.solution_overview:
Adjective + preposition pairs feel flexible when you translate, but exam English treats famous for, similar to, different from, married to, and afraid of as closed locks.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set checks reputation (famous for), comparison (similar to / different from), marriage (married to), and fear (afraid of). With, than, and from transfers are the usual failures.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Cover the preposition and ask which one the adjective textbooks require. If your guess differs from what is on the page, the sentence is false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We arrived to the station just before midnight.
Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.
They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.
Look at the mural behind the café.
We talked the film for almost an hour.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We arrived to the station just before midnight.**

Arrive at a station or building and arrive in a city or country — not arrive to. Get to is the pattern that keeps to.
**B) Please listen to the podcast episode I sent.**

Listen to plus an object is obligatory. Hear can take a direct object; listen cannot in standard exam English.

The podcast line is correctly locked.
**C) They waited the bus for twenty minutes in the rain.**

Wait for someone or something. Wait cannot take the bus as a bare object here.
**D) Look at the mural behind the café.**

Look at directs visual attention to a target. The mural line uses the right preposition.

Watch can take a bare object; look usually needs at.
**E) We talked the film for almost an hour.**

Talk about a topic (or talk to a person). Talk the film drops the required about.
tasks.solution_overview:
Arrive, listen, wait, look, and talk are easy verbs — and easy to strip of the preposition English still needs.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Watch arrive at/in (not to), listen to, wait for, look at, and talk about. Dropping the satellite or using the wrong one after movement and perception verbs is the test.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the verb can take a bare object in standard English. If it cannot, restore the missing preposition before you decide true or false.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She goes to work by foot every morning.
They travelled to the coast by train.
The match starts in Monday evening.
I usually read in night when the house is quiet.
We met on a cold Friday afternoon.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She goes to work by foot every morning.**

Walking uses on foot, not by foot. By is for vehicles (by bus, by train, by car).
**B) They travelled to the coast by train.**

By train correctly names the means of transport. The coast line is fine.
**C) The match starts in Monday evening.**

Days and dated evenings take on: on Monday / on Monday evening. In Monday is wrong.
**D) I usually read in night when the house is quiet.**

At night is the fixed time phrase. Bare in night is not standard.
**E) We met on a cold Friday afternoon.**

On plus a day or date phrase is standard: on a cold Friday afternoon works in everyday and exam English alike.

The adjective cold sits inside the noun phrase and does not change the preposition lock.
tasks.solution_overview:
Time and transport prepositions are closed sets: English picks by, on, in, or at by rule, not by feel.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Remember by + vehicle, on foot (the walking exception), on + day/dated time, and at night. In Monday and in night are classic calendar false friends.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Classify each phrase as transport means or time slot, then apply the closed-set rule instead of translating from another language.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.
Don't blame me about the burnt toast.
Thanks for helping me move the sofa.
The hostel provided us with clean towels.
Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.
tactical_explanations:
**A) We congratulated her for winning the baking contest.**

Congratulate someone on an achievement. For after congratulate is weaker and typically marked wrong in exams.
**B) Don't blame me about the burnt toast.**

Blame someone for something. About does not replace for after blame.
**C) Thanks for helping me move the sofa.**

Thanks for plus a gerund or noun is the correct gratitude frame, and helping fits it cleanly.

Thank someone for doing X follows the same for lock in full-sentence form.
**D) The hostel provided us with clean towels.**

Provide someone with something is the classic ditransitive lock, and clean towels fit it.

Provide something to someone is another acceptable shape; with is right here.
**E) Police charged him of vandalising the bus stop.**

Charge someone with an offence. Of belongs to accuse, not to charge.
tasks.solution_overview:
Speech-act and legal-ish verbs look alike when someone blames, thanks, or charges — but each head keeps its own preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate congratulate on, blame for, thank for, provide with, and charge with. Mixing for/of/about across those heads is the designed trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Identify the speech act first, then recall its private preposition. Near-synonyms do not share satellites.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.
She is fond from old jazz records.
They take pride of their community garden.
I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.
He gets bored of the same playlist every day.
tactical_explanations:
**A) He is keen on early-morning runs along the canal.**

Keen on plus a noun or gerund expresses enthusiasm, same neighbourhood as interested in.

The canal-run line is correctly locked.
**B) She is fond from old jazz records.**

Fond of names people or things you like. Fond from is never the pattern.

Trap: fond from → fond of old jazz records.
**C) They take pride of their community garden.**

Take pride in an achievement. Pride of mixes the noun pride with the adjective proud of.

Trap: take pride of → take pride in their community garden.
**D) I'm tired of waiting for the plumber.**

Tired of plus a gerund or noun is fixed for weariness with a situation.

Exhausted from effort is a different idea with a different preposition.
**E) He gets bored of the same playlist every day.**

Careful English prefers bored with (or by). Bored of is informal and often marked non-standard in exams.

Trap: bored of → bored with the same playlist. (Fed up with is the of-cousin.)
tasks.solution_overview:
Attitude words — keen, fond, pride, tired, bored — each lock to one preposition, and near-synonyms refuse to share.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hold keen on, fond of, take pride in, tired of, and bored with. From/of swaps and informal bored of are the failure modes.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Memorise the pair as a single chunk. If a synonym would take a different preposition, do not import that preposition onto this head.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.
We stayed home because of the flooding.
She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.
In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.
As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.
tactical_explanations:
**A) According to the weather app, storms arrive tonight.**

According to plus a source is the reporting phrase. According with is not used for this meaning.

The weather-app line is correctly formed.
**B) We stayed home because of the flooding.**

Because of plus a noun phrase correctly gives a reason for staying home.

Because + clause would need a finite clause, not of.
**C) She chose tea instead coffee after dinner.**

Instead of coffee is the comparison lock. Bare instead cannot take a following noun this way.

Trap: instead coffee → instead of coffee. (Adverb instead stands alone.)
**D) In addition of stretching, he iced his knee.**

In addition to stretching pairs with as well as — both keep to, not of.
**E) As a result of the delay, they missed the opening act.**

As a result of plus a noun phrase is the fixed causal chunk, and the delay line uses it well.

As a result alone needs a comma and a following clause.
tasks.solution_overview:
Multi-word prepositions are all-or-nothing chunks: miss or swap the final preposition and the whole phrase collapses.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

This set locks according to, because of, instead of, in addition to, and as a result of. Stripped of/to after instead and addition are the main traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Treat each opener as a fixed string. If the last word of the chunk is missing or wrong, mark false without rewriting the rest of the clause.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.
The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.
Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.
Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.
He specialised in marine biology at university.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She insisted that we leave the campsite before dawn.**

Insist that plus a clause is a valid frame alongside insist on + -ing. Leaving before dawn is correctly embedded under that.

Both frames are fine; they are just different shapes.
**B) The coach discouraged them to swim after dark.**

Discourage someone from swimming, not to swim. The from + -ing pattern matches prevent and keep.
**C) Warm soup helped him recover from the cold.**

Recover from an illness is the standard medical collocation. Recover of is wrong.

The warm-soup line stands.
**D) Nothing will stop her to finish the marathon.**

For prevention, stop someone from finishing (or stop someone finishing). Stop her to finish means pause in order to finish — the wrong reading here.
**E) He specialised in marine biology at university.**

Specialise in a field is fixed. Marine biology at university fits the lock.
tasks.solution_overview:
Some verbs invite an infinitive that is actually illegal — they want from + -ing, or a that-clause instead.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep insist that (alongside insist on), recover from, and specialise in. Catch discourage and preventive stop, which take from + -ing rather than to-infinitives.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

When a verb seems to take to + V, pause: is it really a prevent/encourage family member that wants from + -ing? Check that family first.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I'm used to waking up before sunrise.
She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.
They are accustomed with long bus rides.
He prefers walking to cycling in the city.
We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I'm used to waking up before sunrise.**

Be/get used to plus a gerund means accustomed to a habit. Waking before sunrise fits that familiarity frame.
**B) She used to waking up before sunrise when she worked nights.**

Past habit needs used to + base verb: used to wake, not used to waking.

Trap: used to waking → used to wake when she worked nights. Do not confuse with be used to + -ing.
**C) They are accustomed with long bus rides.**

Accustomed to mirrors used to for familiarity. Accustomed with is wrong.

Trap: accustomed with → accustomed to long bus rides.
**D) He prefers walking to cycling in the city.**

Prefer X to Y correctly stacks two options: walking to cycling.

That to comparison is the standard exam shape; than would belong to rather, not prefer.
**E) We prefer walking than cycling when it rains.**

Prefer … than is not the English comparison. Use prefer walking to cycling, or would rather walk than cycle.
highlights: used to waking up before sunrise when
tasks.solution_overview:
Used to and be used to look like the same phrase; prefer … to/than collides the same way. This task forces you to keep the frames apart.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Separate past-habit used to + base verb from be used to + -ing, keep accustomed to, and compare with prefer A to B — never prefer … than.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask first whether used to means past habit or present familiarity. Then check prefer comparisons for to versus than.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.
In spite the heat, they finished the hike.
Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.
She refrained to comment during the argument.
Please refrain from posting spoilers online.
tactical_explanations:
**A) In spite of the heat, they finished the hike.**

In spite of plus a noun phrase equals despite. The of is part of the chunk, and the hike line keeps it.
**B) In spite the heat, they finished the hike.**

In spite must be followed by of before a noun. In spite the heat is incomplete.
**C) Notwithstanding the late start, the choir sounded polished.**

Notwithstanding takes a noun phrase with no extra of, like despite. The choir line is correct.
**D) She refrained to comment during the argument.**

Refrain from commenting, not refrain to comment. Abstain follows the same from + -ing shape.
**E) Please refrain from posting spoilers online.**

Refrain from plus a gerund is the fixed restraint pattern, and posting spoilers fits it.

Keep from after refrain; a to-infinitive would break the same head you fixed in the previous false line.
tasks.solution_overview:
Contrast markers and restraint verbs look interchangeable until you notice which ones keep of and which ones refuse it.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Despite and notwithstanding take a noun with no of; in spite of needs of. Refrain takes from + -ing, not a to-infinitive.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For contrast phrases, check whether of is required or forbidden. For refrain, demand from + -ing every time.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.
Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.
She has no intention to cancel the trip.
There is no point of arguing about the score.
What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?
tactical_explanations:
**A) The outcome of the experiment depends on temperature.**

Depend on correctly ties the outcome to temperature. Outcome of X and depend on Y can both be right in one sentence.
**B) Access to the roof terrace is restricted after dusk.**

Access to a place is the fixed pattern for entry rights. Access of is not used for places.
**C) She has no intention to cancel the trip.**

Have no intention of cancelling is the preferred exam lock. Intention to is often marked wrong even when heard elsewhere.
**D) There is no point of arguing about the score.**

No point in arguing is the frame here. Point of arguing mismatches this no-point structure (though what's the point of is a related pattern).
**E) What's the point in staying if the museum is closed?.**

What's the point in staying matches an acceptable rhetorical frame with in + gerund.

Point in and point of both appear; match the whole fixed question shape.
tasks.solution_overview:
Abstract nouns — outcome, access, intention, point — each pick a locked preposition that does not follow from "future" intuition alone.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Keep depend on and access to. Prefer intention of + -ing and match point in/of to the whole fixed frame; bare intention to is the soft trap.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Do not assume to after every noun that looks ahead. Check the collocation dictionary pattern for that noun before judging.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.
He was angry about the cancelled ferry.
They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.
I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.
We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She was angry with her brother for borrowing her headphones.**

Angry with a person plus for a reason is a solid double pattern: with her brother for borrowing the headphones.

With names the person; for names the offence — both locks can sit in one sentence.

**Tip:** ** Angry with people; about situations.
**B) He was angry about the cancelled ferry.**

Angry about a cancelled ferry correctly targets a situation or event, not a person.

If the complement were a sibling or colleague, you would switch to angry with instead.

**Tip:** ** About for things; with for people.
**C) They were pleased of the surprise birthday brunch.**

Pleased with or by — not pleased of. Proud of is the of-cousin; do not import it onto pleased.
**D) I'm delighted with how the garden turned out.**

Delighted with a result is natural and grammatical. Delighted by also works; delighted to hear that… is another frame.
**E) We were surprised from the sudden snowfall.**

Surprised by or at the news — not surprised from.
tasks.solution_overview:
Emotion adjectives split people from situations, and they reject of/from transfers that proud sometimes invites.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Use angry with for people and angry about for situations; keep pleased/delighted with and surprised by/at. Pleased of and surprised from are the traps.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the complement is a person or a situation, then lock the preposition. Reject of/from unless the adjective truly owns them (proud of, not pleased of).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.
This jacket smells like woodsmoke.
She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.
Can you remind me of locking the back door?
Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The soup tastes of garlic and lemon.**

Taste of a flavour is the fixed sensory pattern for substances in the soup.

Smell of works the same way for a substance.
**B) This jacket smells like woodsmoke.**

Smell like for resemblance is acceptable and grammatical here.

Smell of woodsmoke would also work as a substance reading.
**C) She reminded me of my primary-school teacher.**

Remind someone of a person or thing triggers memory or resemblance. The teacher line uses of correctly.

**Tip:** ** Remind of a memory; remind to do a duty.
**D) Can you remind me of locking the back door?.**

For a future action, remind me to lock — not remind me of locking. Of would suggest memory or resemblance, not a prompt.
**E) Please remind him to bring the picnic blanket.**

Remind someone to plus an infinitive correctly issues a prompt about a future action.

That to-frame is the instruction reading; of would be for memory or resemblance, not for "bring the blanket."

**Tip:** ** Reminder for actions → to + V.
tasks.solution_overview:
Sensory of/like patterns are usually safe; remind is the hard verb because it splits into two different frames.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Taste of and smell like are fine for flavour and resemblance. Remind of covers memory or resemblance; remind to covers a future prompt — do not mix them.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For remind, ask whether the complement is a memory trigger or an instruction to act. That single question chooses of versus to.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.
Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.
The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.
Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.
Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The festival was cancelled owing to high winds.**

Owing to plus a noun phrase is a formal because-of equivalent. High winds fit the causal slot.
**B) Owing the high winds, the festival was cancelled.**

Owing needs to before the noun phrase. Bare Owing the… is incomplete.

Trap: insert to → Owing to the high winds.
**C) The hike was postponed due to flooding on the trail.**

Due to plus a noun is widely accepted as a causal preposition in modern exam English, matching because of.

Flooding on the trail fills that noun slot, so the postponed-hike line stands.
**D) Due the flooding, the hike was postponed.**

Due the flooding drops the required to.
**E) Thanks to a clear sky, we saw the meteor shower.**

Thanks to plus a noun credits a (usually positive) cause. Clear sky and meteor shower fit that shade.

**Tip:** ** Thanks to (positive); owing/due to (neutral/negative).
tasks.solution_overview:
Causal multi-word prepositions all keep a final to: strip it and the phrase is broken even if the nouns are clear.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Owing to, due to, and thanks to are complete only with to. Owing the… and Due the… are automatic fails; the full forms with to are true.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Scan for owing/due/thanks and confirm the next word is to. Missing to alone decides false.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 18
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: She accused him for leaving the gate open.
They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.
He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.
The club banned him from using the tennis courts.
Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.
tactical_explanations:
**A) She accused him for leaving the gate open.**

Accuse someone of doing, not for. For belongs to blame.

Trap: accused him for → accused him of leaving the gate open.
**B) They suspected her of feeding the stray cats.**

Suspected of plus a gerund is the fixed collocation for alleged wrongdoing.

The same of satellite appears after accuse; do not swap in for here.
**C) He was convicted for trespassing on farmland.**

Convicted of an offence is the standard legal/exam pattern. For appears in loose usage but of is the safer lock here.
**D) The club banned him from using the tennis courts.**

Ban someone from plus a gerund or noun is correct. Prohibit follows from; forbid someone to is a different shape.
**E) Nothing can compensate the loss of the old oak.**

Compensate for a loss. In this sense compensate cannot take the loss as a bare object.

Trap: compensate the loss → compensate for the loss of the old oak.
tasks.solution_overview:
Fault, suspicion, conviction, bans, and compensation are preposition-heavy: one wrong satellite and the legal flavour collapses.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Hold accuse/suspect/convict of, ban from, and compensate for. Accuse for, convict for, and bare compensate the loss are the designed errors.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Pair each verb with its private preposition before you care about the gerund. Dropping or swapping that satellite fails the item.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 19
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.
Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.
She prides herself in finishing every crossword.
She takes pride in finishing every crossword.
He is proud for his daughter's science prize.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The plan is contingent on dry weather this weekend.**

Contingent on plus a noun or gerund matches depend on for conditions. Dry weather fits.
**B) Approval is contingent of dry weather this weekend.**

Contingent of is a depend-of style transfer. The condition lock is on.
**C) She prides herself in finishing every crossword.**

Pride oneself on doing, not in, after the reflexive verb. In belongs to take pride in.

Trap: prides herself in → prides herself on finishing every crossword.
**D) She takes pride in finishing every crossword.**

Take pride in plus a gerund is fixed and correct here.

Be proud of is the adjective cousin with of.
**E) He is proud for his daughter's science prize.**

Proud of an achievement, not proud for.

Trap: proud for → proud of his daughter's science prize.
tasks.solution_overview:
Pride frames look identical until you notice the verb under them: pride oneself, take pride, and be proud each want a different preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Contingent follows depend → on (never of). Then separate pride oneself on, take pride in, and be proud of — importing in/for across those frames fails.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Name the exact verb phrase first. Only then pick on, in, or of. Contingent always tracks depend on.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 20
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.
The café had run out from cups before noon.
I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.
She objects to being photographed without consent.
He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.
tactical_explanations:
**A) By the time we arrived, the café had run out of cups.**

Run out of plus a noun is the depletion pattern. Cups before arrival fits of.
**B) The café had run out from cups before noon.**

Run out from cups is wrong; materials take of after run out.
**C) I'm looking forward for the weekend hike.**

Looking forward to the hike, not for. To is part of the multi-word verb and takes a noun or -ing.
**D) She objects to being photographed without consent.**

Object to plus a gerund is correct: objects to being photographed. Against is a false friend from other languages.
**E) He succeeded on repairing the leaky tap.**

Succeeded in repairing, not on. On belongs to insist, not succeed.

Trap: succeeded on → succeeded in repairing the leaky tap.
tasks.solution_overview:
Close with the high-frequency exam cluster: run out, look forward, object, and succeed — each fails or passes on one satellite preposition.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Lock run out of, look forward to, object to, and succeed in. From/for/on swaps are the only difference between true and false here.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ignore how natural the sentence feels in translation. Match the exact multi-word verb to its textbook preposition, then decide.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE
